rules.gameRulesDescription: Historical Spy is a deduction game where players must identify spies, while spies must hide their role.
rules.playerDescription: Players see the answer on the card—a term, historical figure, or event from Belarusian school textbooks on world history and the history of Belarus—and must help others guess it without saying it outright. Goal: identify and exile all spies.
rules.spyDescription: Spies don't know the answer on the card and must pretend they do to avoid being identified. Goal: remain undetected or have spies equal to or outnumber players.
rules.step1: Set up the game: choose the number of players, spies, and round time (or infinite time).
rules.step2: Each player takes turns looking at their card. Regular players see the clue (term, name, or event); spies only see their role.
rules.step3: Players discuss and ask questions, trying to identify spies. Use the timer to control discussion time.
rules.step4: At any time, you can exile a suspected player. If a spy is exiled, they're out. If a player is exiled, the game continues.
rules.playersWinDescription: If all spies have been identified and exiled, players win.
rules.spiesWinDescription: If the number of remaining spies equals or exceeds the number of remaining players, or if time runs out before all spies are found, spies win.
rules.tip1: Players: lean on the curriculum and typical textbook passages on world history and the history of Belarus—without saying the card answer verbatim.
rules.tip2: Spies: listen to the discussion and reconstruct the answer as if skimming a textbook—timelines, maps, diagrams, glossaries, and illustration captions.
rules.tip3: Use exile tactics strategically—don't rush to exile too early.
rules.tip4: Pay attention to other players' behavior—who is too confident or too uncertain in their answers?
rules.questionTopicsDescription: All answers come from Belarusian school textbooks on world history and the history of Belarus: the card may be a term, a historical figure, or an event. Adapt the prompts below to the set you are playing—just avoid saying the full card answer aloud: others gain hints while the spy does not.
rules.questionTopic1: Which state, people, or political camp is this tied to in the textbook?
rules.questionTopic2: Which capital, court, or map region is this linked to in a paragraph or diagram?
rules.questionTopic3: Which century and school-timeline slot is this usually taught in—antiquity, Middle Ages, early modern, or modern history?
rules.questionTopic4: In the syllabus, is this mainly a person, an event, a term or institution, a reform, or a cultural phenomenon?
rules.questionTopic5: On which continent or historical region does the book place this next to a map?
rules.questionTopic6: Does this appear in a unit on a major war, campaign, revolution, or liberation movement?
rules.questionTopic7: Is this tied to taking power, how the state is organized, losing independence, or restoring sovereignty?
rules.questionTopic8: How is this named in a source excerpt, chronicle, glossary, or illustration caption?
rules.questionTopic9: In the course, is this remembered more for a battle, a date, a law, a discovery, or a religious or cultural role?
rules.questionTopic10: How many dates, stages, titles, or conceptual layers does the topic attach to this?
rules.questionTopic11: Which dynasty, date, or era label is this most often paired with in a "match the pairs" task?
rules.questionTopic12: In the book, is this under rulers, war and campaigns, culture, or a block of terms and definitions?
rules.questionTopic13: Does this fit one paragraph or span a whole subheading in the contents?
rules.questionTopic14: Which event, date, or context opens the explanation in the school narrative?
rules.questionTopic15: Is this a world-history theme or a "History of Belarus" section (Kievan Rus', GDL, Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, modern and contemporary times)?
rules.questionTopic16: How many key outcomes, wins, or defeats are tied to this in the lesson text?
rules.questionTopic17: Does this show up when the book covers colonies, empires, national liberation, or border defense?
rules.questionTopic18: Is this connected with a coronation, constitution, republic, award, or the label "symbol of the age" in the program?
rules.questionTopic19: Which single episode, document, date, or diagram makes this "must-memorize" in the textbook?
rules.questionTopic20: With what—or whom—from neighboring paragraphs is this compared on a table or timeline?
rules.questionTopic21: In which language does the course quote this, name an act or a work, when that applies?
rules.questionTopic22: Which battle, front line, route, or plan is this tied to in an illustration or on a map?
rules.questionTopic23: In which war, revolution, or crisis is this a central node or a secondary detail for the textbook?
rules.questionTopic24: What span of time covers the action, the law's validity, or the event chronology in the chunk you study in class?
rules.questionTopic25: Is this cited when discussing economy, trade, reparations, or a "legacy" for later generations?
rules.questionTopic26: In which country or on which lands—including historical regions of Belarus—does this happen or apply per the syllabus?
rules.questionTopic27: Is this linked to uniting states, an empire breaking up, a peace treaty, or redrawn borders on the textbook map?
rules.questionTopic28: At which point in the school course (grade, unit, chronology block) is this usually taught?
rules.questionTopic29: Which capital, state, monument, or symbol is this tied to in a lesson on identity and culture?
rules.questionTopic30: With which other examples from the "key terms, figures, or dates" list is this placed side by side for memorization?
